Date: 2027-02-17
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Sam Patel (Redwood AE), Ingrid Cho (Redwood SE), Alex Morgan (OceanPay - Head of ML), Priya Singh (OceanPay - Platform), Dmitri Kozlov (OceanPay - SRE)
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked OceanPay through Redwood Optimize recommendations focused on batching and prefix/KV cache. Main topics: cost/latency tradeoffs, caching strategies for payment-related prompts, estimation model for token savings, and POC next steps (benchmarks + traffic share). Customer concerned about PII, KMS, and VPC/private deployment for compliance; discussed hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs.
topics: Prefix vs KV cache behaviors and hit rates
Cost model: tokens saved, CPU/GPU utilization, throughput impact
Latency SLOs and tail latency tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Sam Patel: Hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Sam from Redwood, and engineer Ingrid is with me, say hi Ingrid.
[00:07] Ingrid Cho: Hi all, thanks for the time, we know you sent over the traffic sample, thanks Alex for that.
[00:13] Alex Morgan: Yeah no problem, quick note, some of the traces are partially anonymized cause of PCI stuff so hope that's OK.
[00:20] Priya Singh: right, we can't share card data, so it's masked.
[00:27] Sam Patel: Totally expected. Today we'll focus on Optimize — batching and prefix/KV cache recommendations plus a simple cost model so you can see unit economics. We'll keep it practical.
[00:38] Ingrid Cho: Quick agenda: 1) how batching works in our runtime, 2) prefix cache vs KV cache tradeoffs, 3) cost model and example numbers, 4) POC plan.
[00:47] Dmitri Kozlov: Sounds good. curious about tail latency if we batch aggressively.
[00:52] Ingrid Cho: Great callout. So first, batching — we support a continuous batching pipeline that groups requests arriving within a small window and on similar sequence lengths. The goal is to improve GPU utilization without blowing past your latency SLO.
[01:08] Sam Patel: For example, if your SLO is 150ms p95, we recommend conservative micro-batching (8-32) depending on prompt length; that often reduces cost per token by ~20-40% for high-concurrency workloads.
[01:22] Alex Morgan: 20-40% is promising. How do you compute that?
[01:26] Ingrid Cho: We model GPU utilization + kernel efficiency. In the cost model we show baseline per-token cost on host versus after batching and with caching — it's a combined effect. We'll share the spreadsheet.
[01:36] Priya Singh: What about cold start for KV caches? if we route to a fresh instance does it miss a lot?
[01:42] Ingrid Cho: Yes there is a cold period. The KV cache is per-session on the server runtime; when you have long-lived sessions or repeated prefixes we get high hit rates. For stateless API calls, prefix cache sits in the edge cache layer and can hit regardless of session, but TTLs matter.
[01:55] Sam Patel: To clarify prefix vs KV: prefix cache is content-addressed caching of repeated prompt prefixes (good for templates, system prompts). KV cache stores past key/values for a token stream to avoid recomputing attention for continuation — that helps long convo latencies and reduces compute on subsequent tokens.
[02:12] Alex Morgan: So KV helps when users keep the chat open? we mostly have ephemeral sessions but reuse system prompt and product description templates.
[02:20] Ingrid Cho: That's exactly the mix where both help: prefix cache catches the repeated system prompts and templates, KV helps if you have multi-turn within short timeframe — even a few seconds of reuse matter.
[02:29] Dmitri Kozlov: Any numbers on hit rates? heuristics?
[02:33] Ingrid Cho: In our experience across payments customers, prefix hit rates vary widely: 5-60% depending on templating. In the demo deck we put conservative estimates: 15% typical, 35% good, 55% exceptional. KV cache hit rate depends on session stickiness; with 5-10s sticky sessions you might see 10-25% effective token reuse.
[02:52] Sam Patel: So cost model: assume baseline cost $0.0025 per 1k tokens on this open model variant (demo numbers). If batching reduces compute 30% and caching saves 20% tokens, combined you can see ~44% TCO drop (1 - (0.7 * 0.8)). These are illustrative — we'll run your traces for accurate numbers.
[03:18] Alex Morgan: That math helps. Are these numbers different on Dedicated vs Hosted?
[03:23] Ingrid Cho: Good question. Dedicated gives more predictable throughput and you can tune instance types and quantization, so unit costs in committed capacity are lower but upfront. Hosted is more flexible; we can simulate both in the spreadsheet.
[03:34] Priya Singh: On the security side — we need to know about KMS integration and audit logs for caching. If cached content contains PII, how do you control that?
[03:44] Sam Patel: Redwood supports KMS/HSM integrations and you can set cache policies per route. For PCI-sensitive routes we recommend disabling prefix cache or encrypting cached blobs with customer-managed keys. We'll send the security whitepaper and cookie settings; we also have SOC2 reports.
[04:01] Alex Morgan: Do you support VPC/private deployment for those routes only?
[04:05] Ingrid Cho: Yes, we have private deployments and VPC peering so traffic and persistence can be isolated. Some customers run a hybrid where sensitive endpoints go to Private and lower-risk flows use Hosted.
[04:16] Dmitri Kozlov: Ok. Back to batching — how do you tune maximum batch size? do you test with our trace?
[04:21] Ingrid Cho: We'll simulate your inter-arrival times and prompt length distribution. In practice we recommend a policy: target p95 latency by adjusting batch timeout and max batch size. For example, if most requests are short (<64 tokens) and concurrency >200, a max batch of 32 with 15ms buffer is OK.
[04:38] Alex Morgan: Do you do dynamic batching automatically? like increase batch size when backlog grows?
[04:41] Ingrid Cho: Yes, runtime does continuous batching and adapts, but you can lock to policies per route. We expose metrics in Console so you can see effective batch sizes and tail latencies.
[04:51] Sam Patel: I'll point out a common tradeoff — aggressive batching helps cost but can add tens of milliseconds to p95 if traffic is bursty. So for payment flows where latency is critical, we prefer prefix cache and smaller batches. For lower-critical flows like batch reconciliation or reporting, you can push bigger batches.
[05:08] Priya Singh: What's the impact on throughput (rps) when caching is enabled?
[05:12] Ingrid Cho: Good caching can increase effective throughput since fewer tokens are executed, so GPU cycles are freed. In some cases we've seen effective throughput double on high-template workloads.
[05:21] Alex Morgan: Example: we have 120 rps at peak, median prompt 180 tokens, system prompt 80 tokens repeated. What ballpark savings could we expect?
[05:33] Ingrid Cho: With a repeated 80-token system prompt, prefix cache could save ~30-40% tokens if it hits; batching maybe 25-35% depending on concurrency and sequence length mixing. Combined, conservative estimate ~40% cost reduction; optimistic up to 60% for well-structured templates. We'll run your trace to firm numbers.
[05:55] Dmitri Kozlov: For the POC, how do you instrument to show cache hit rate and token savings?
[05:59] Sam Patel: Console has per-route metrics: cache hit rate, tokens served, effective batch sizes, latency p50/p95/p99. We'll provide a dashboard template and an exportable CSV for the POC.
[06:11] Priya Singh: You mentioned TTLs for prefix cache — what defaults and can we tune per-route?
[06:16] Ingrid Cho: Defaults are 5 minutes for prefix cache, but you can set route-specific TTLs or rules to never cache certain tokens (PII indicators). KV cache is session-based and evicts based on LRU and memory pressure.
[06:30] Alex Morgan: How do you handle cache invalidation if templates change?
[06:34] Ingrid Cho: You can bump a template version in the prompt metadata which invalidates entries, and Console exposes a 'purge cache' action per route.
[06:41] Sam Patel: On costs — we'll provide both hosted per-token model and dedicated reserved pricing scenarios in the spreadsheet. For dedicated we show amortized GPU cost, and you can see break-even at X rps (we'll compute).
[06:55] Alex Morgan: Any limits on cache size or do you charge for cache storage?
[06:58] Ingrid Cho: Cache storage is included in the service for typical usage; for very large key-value tables we can discuss large object storage options and pricing. We'll flag that in the spreadsheet if needed.
[07:10] Priya Singh: Can we run a small live test — route some subset of traffic?
[07:13] Sam Patel: Absolutely. Typical POC: we run a 2-week test with a mirror of a fraction of traffic or recorded trace run. Ingrid will run the trace in the Optimize sandbox and produce a savings report.
[07:24] Dmitri Kozlov: How do you mirror traffic safely without sending PII?
[07:28] Ingrid Cho: We recommend sanitization/masking at source — you can use our local capture tooling or provide masked traces. For the mirror we can discard payloads after processing and keep metrics only. We'll detail the exact pipeline in the POC doc.
[07:43] Alex Morgan: On compliance — you said KMS, SOC2. Do you support customer-managed keys for prefix cache encryption?
[07:49] Sam Patel: Yes. We can encrypt cache blobs at rest with customer-managed KMS keys and provide audit logs. That's a common requirement for finance customers.
[07:58] Priya Singh: Do you log raw prompts? we need to control retention.
[08:02] Ingrid Cho: You can configure retention and redaction; Console shows token counts without storing raw text unless enabled. We'll provide the retention settings doc.
[08:12] Alex Morgan: Ok good. Back to tuning: any heuristics for prompts with dynamic sections, e.g., order IDs embed — cache still useful?
[08:20] Ingrid Cho: If the variable portion is at the end of the prompt, prefix cache still helps for the static head. For highly dynamic prefixes, hit rate falls, so consider template extraction: move constant text to system prompt and send variables separately.
[08:33] Dmitri Kozlov: That might require client changes.
[08:36] Priya Singh: We're open to small SDK changes if it saves cost.
[08:39] Sam Patel: Great. We'll include sample SDK snippets for template extraction.
[08:44] Ingrid Cho: Quick demo screen share: here's Console's Optimize panel, route-level metrics, and the cost model tab — (demoed table) — the spreadsheet shows baseline tokens, cached tokens, effective GPU-seconds, and estimated monthly cost.
[09:05] Alex Morgan: I see an "estimated savings" column. How reliable is it?
[09:09] Ingrid Cho: It's an estimate based on sample traces and conservative hit-rate assumptions; we flag a range (low/expected/high). The POC will firm numbers.
[09:18] Priya Singh: For the POC, what's the instrumentation we need to drop in?
[09:22] Sam Patel: 1) route mapping so we can apply policies, 2) sample traces (masked), 3) list of critical SLOs and success metrics. We'll also ask for a short-living service account so our SE can spin up a sandbox.
[09:34] Alex Morgan: Timeline expectation?
[09:36] Sam Patel: We can do a 2-week run after we receive the traces and service account. Prep is typically 2-3 business days. So overall 3 weeks to delivery of the POC report.
[09:46] Dmitri Kozlov: Any red flags on our side from the sample we looked at?
[09:50] Ingrid Cho: Not yet; your templates are fairly structured which is good. We'll confirm after running the trace.
[09:56] Alex Morgan: Pricing: your hosted numbers above were $0.0025 per 1k tokens — do you have real tiers for production?
[10:03] Sam Patel: That's demo pricing. We'll include actual per-token tiers and dedicated reserved options in the pricing sheet. Also note that with Dedicated you get lower per-token compute and can enable more aggressive quantization for additional savings.
[10:17] Priya Singh: What about model variants — could we route to a cheaper model for reconciliation flows?
[10:22] Ingrid Cho: Absolutely. Smart routing can send flows to cheaper variants or quantized models and fallback to higher quality only when needed. You can set policies per route in Console.
[10:32] Alex Morgan: Any issues with output quality when using KV cache or batching?
[10:36] Ingrid Cho: No correctness impact from caching — KV cache avoids recomputation of attention but doesn't change model outputs. Batching is transparent; the only quality change would be if you switch model variants or quantize more aggressively. We recommend evals and quality monitoring during POC.
[10:51] Sam Patel: We'll also set up regression alerts tied to your prompt-suite so any drift is caught.
[10:56] Alex Morgan: Nice. One more on metrics — can we get per-customer tenant dashboards?
[11:00] Ingrid Cho: Yes per-route and per-tenant breakdowns. You can also export token-level billing for reconciliation.
[11:07] Priya Singh: Ok, let's recap next steps.
[11:10] Sam Patel: Recap: 1) Sam sends spreadsheet + pricing, 2) Ingrid runs trace-based simulation and shares POC plan, 3) OceanPay shares masked traces and SLOs, 4) schedule POC kickoff next week.
[11:23] Alex Morgan: That works. I'll share the traces today, Priya will coordinate.
[11:27] Priya Singh: I'll send them by EOD tomorrow.
[11:31] Dmitri Kozlov: Any blockers on our side for sandbox creds?
[11:34] Sam Patel: Just a short-lived service account with limited scope; Ingrid will send exact requirements.
[11:40] Ingrid Cho: I'll email the sample config and SDK snippet after the call.
[11:44] Alex Morgan: Thanks everyone, that was helpful.
[11:47] Sam Patel: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the materials and schedule.
[11:50] Priya Singh: Thanks.
[11:52] (call ends)

Notes: Transcript contains occasional ASR artifacts and paraphrasing; speaker labels are a mix of role and name. References to pricing are illustrative and not contractual.
